purpose: Which rectangle keeps the same aspect ratio after removing a square?
meaning: A golden rectangle has a long-to-short ratio φ greater than one such that removing a square leaves a rotated rectangle with the same ratio. The equality φ=1/(φ−1) gives φ²=φ+1 and φ=(1+√5)/2. Ratios of consecutive Fibonacci numbers supply finite rational comparisons.

definition.setting: A designer cuts a square from a rectangular panel. In a golden rectangle the remaining rectangle, turned a quarter turn, has the original proportions. Compare its exact ratio with ratios of consecutive Fibonacci numbers.

signature.φ: Exact golden ratio, the root greater than one of φ²=φ+1
signature.L: Long side of the golden panel, in metres
signature.w: Width left after removing the square, in metres
signature.Δ: Finite ratio minus the golden ratio

conditions: The short side is 0.5 to 3 metres. The positive ratio greater than one solves φ²=φ+1. Fibonacci index k is a whole number from 2 to 12, with F(1)=F(2)=1. A finite Fibonacci ratio is an approximation, not the exact golden ratio. No claim about universal beauty, nature or optimal design follows.

properties.claim: A golden rectangle has a long-to-short ratio φ greater than one such that removing a square leaves a rotated rectangle with the same ratio. The equality φ=1/(φ−1) gives φ²=φ+1 and φ=(1+√5)/2. Ratios of consecutive Fibonacci numbers supply finite rational comparisons.

properties.derivation: Let the long-to-short ratio be φ=L/s>1. After removing an s-by-s square, the remaining dimensions are s and L−s. Requiring the rotated remainder to be similar gives L/s=s/(L−s), hence φ(φ−1)=1 and φ²−φ−1=0. The positive root greater than one is (1+√5)/2. Fibonacci numbers satisfy F(k+1)=F(k)+F(k−1); the shown ratios are rational approximations. This finite display does not by itself prove convergence.
